problem:
A cargo crate of mass $55\,\text{kg}$ is projected vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the crate's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the crate is proportional to their velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=22\,\text{kg/s}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g$, and the only forces acting on the crate are the weight due to gravity and drag.

feedback.problem:
A storage module of mass $60\,\text{kg}$ is projected vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the module's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the module is proportional to their velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=15\,\text{kg/s}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g$, and the only forces acting on the module are the weight due to gravity and drag.
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, there are two forces acting on the storage module:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the module, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =60g\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity of the module (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-kv=-15v
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the module is

$$
F=w+D=60g-15v.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the module, we have

$$
60g-15v=60\,\frac{dv}{dt}.
$$

Finally, simplifying and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}60\,\frac{dv}{dt}+15v & =60g \\ \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{1}{4}v & =g.\end{aligned}
$$
